name: gateway
intent: Wrap all access to an external system or resource in an object whose interface speaks the local application's vocabulary, so foreign APIs, protocols and data shapes stay behind one translation point instead of spreading through the code.
problem: Every call site that talks to a foreign system has to know that system's API: awkward types, transport details, authentication, serialisation, paging and error conventions. That foreign vocabulary leaks into business code, so a change on the outside (new version, different endpoint, another vendor) becomes a scattered edit, and ordinary logic cannot be tested without reaching the real remote resource.
context: A boundary where the other side is not under your control: a remote service over HTTP/gRPC, a relational or legacy data store reached with SQL, a vendor SDK, a file format or a device. The pattern applies whenever the foreign API is awkward from the caller's viewpoint - different types, units, identifiers, dates or error model - and there is more than a trivial one-line call to contain.
benefits: All foreign vocabulary is confined to one object: callers read as local operations ('listBoneFusionSlots') instead of transport and API details.
A single place absorbs external change - vendor, version, endpoint, wire format, error model - so the blast radius of a foreign API change stays inside the gateway.
The optional connection object gives a clean test seam: a test double replaces the remote call, so tests stay fast and deterministic without touching the real service.
Cross-cutting concerns (authentication, retries, timeouts, metrics, caching, mapping) are applied once and uniformly instead of being re-derived at every call site.
Swapping, shielding or version-pinning an external system becomes a local refactoring; the domain keeps its own types and its own language.
Design pressure at the boundary: forcing translation exposes foreign concepts that would otherwise creep into the domain model, which is how a gateway implements an anti-corruption layer.
tradeoffs: An extra layer of indirection and code to maintain: for a clean API with a single call site the gateway costs more than it removes.

A second vocabulary must be maintained: someone has to decide, per foreign concept, whether to translate it or adopt the foreign term (Fowler's Conformist-versus-anti-corruption-layer judgement), and an unowned translation drifts.
Translation drift and invisibility: fields and capabilities added by the foreign system stay invisible until the gateway exposes them, so the gateway becomes a gatekeeper for external change.
The ergonomic interface invites chatty use: a per-row loop hidden behind one innocent-looking method turns an obvious N+1 network pattern into invisible cost.
Stubbing the connection means the translation itself is not exercised by unit tests; without at least one contract test against the real counterpart, assumptions about the foreign API rot silently.
A gateway that leaks foreign types in its signature - or lets business rules in - is worse than no abstraction: callers end up coupled to both vocabularies and the seam is no longer testable.

participants.responsibility: Application code that uses the gateway; knows only the domestic interface and the local value types, never the foreign API, its types or its error model.

Declares the operations the application needs in domestic terms and translates arguments, results and failures to and from the foreign API; contains translation only, no application policy or business rules.

Optional but standard for remote gateways: a thin wrapper around the mechanics of the foreign call - endpoint, protocol, headers, authentication, serialisation, completion - and the substitution point for test doubles.
The (possibly inline) conversion between foreign payloads and domestic types: field renaming, unit and date conversion, identifier mapping, enrichment from local data, error-code mapping.
The external service, data source, vendor library or file format being accessed; it defines the foreign vocabulary and knows nothing about the gateway.

use_cases: Wrapping a partner or vendor REST/gRPC service behind operations named in the application's language (payments, shipping, booking, identity, video metadata).
Accessing a relational or legacy resource: JDBC/JPA/ADO.NET/psycopg code that owns the SQL for one table or data source and maps rows into domestic objects (the table data gateway form).
Legacy and non-object resources — CICS/terminal transactions, SOAP endpoints, XML or CSV feeds, device and file interfaces — whose idioms are nothing like the application's.
Making boundary code testable: substituting the connection object so business logic runs without a remote call, and keeping contract tests against the real service for the mapping itself.
Insulating a domain from a third-party SDK whose types and error model must not appear in domain code — a gateway used as an anti-corruption layer.
Centralising endpoint configuration, credentials, retries, rate-limit handling and observability for one external system in one owned place.
GraphQL subgraph gateway: exposing a federated supergraph schema to clients while translating resolver calls into downstream REST/gRPC/messaging service calls.
Event-driven integration: a messaging gateway wrapping a message broker (Kafka, SQS, RabbitMQ) so producers and consumers speak in domain events rather than queue primitives.
Multi-tenant SaaS isolation: a per-tenant gateway instance that injects tenant-specific credentials, base URLs and feature flags, keeping the translation logic shared.
Database view gateway: a thin SQL gateway that maps one or more database views into domain objects, shielding callers from schema evolution and join complexity.
gRPC microservice boundary: a gateway that translates HTTP/REST from an API edge into idiomatic gRPC calls and maps error codes back to domain error types.
Rate-limited partner API: a gateway that manages a token bucket or sliding-window rate limiter, queues or rejects excess requests, and maps rate-limit 429 responses into domestic retry-after errors.

Spring Integration's Messaging Gateway (@MessagingGateway or GatewayProxyFactoryBean) exposes a small application-facing interface while hiding the framework's messaging API; use it as a local connection boundary, keeping domain policy outside it.

At a provider edge, Azure API Management and Amazon API Gateway proxy requests and centralise credentials, quotas, transformations and telemetry; use these infrastructure gateways for shared traffic concerns while keeping consumer-side foreign-vocabulary translation in a client-owned gateway.

Kubernetes Gateway API's Gateway and HTTPRoute resources centralise listener and routing policy to Services; keep application-level translation and domain errors behind a separate gateway rather than putting business rules in route configuration.
avoid_when: The foreign API is already clean and pervasive (language collections, standard streams, platform facilities): wrapping it only adds a vocabulary nobody asked for; use the platform API directly.
A single call site with a straightforward API and no testing need: a direct call, or one thin wrapper function, is simpler than a gateway object.
The real problem is chatty fine-grained interaction that must be aggregated into fewer remote calls: use Remote Facade (a coarse-grained interface) rather than a thin per-call gateway.
You own both sides and the foreign service should speak your domain directly: publish an Open Host Service with a DTO contract instead of translating per client.
The payload merely has to be packaged for transport, not translated: Data Transfer Object is the smaller and sufficient answer.
anti_patterns: Gateway as a god object: one class wrapping every external system, so unrelated foreign vocabularies share one file, one failure domain and one owner.
Business logic inside the gateway (pricing, application validation, orchestration): clients then depend on the gateway for decisions it should not own.
Leaking foreign types — vendor DTOs, connection objects, raw JSON or result sets — out of gateway methods, so callers are coupled to both vocabularies.
Per-client translation drift: several independently written gateways to the same service with different mappings, so behaviour depends on which caller you ask.
Confusing the client-side gateway with a provider-side API gateway (a facade the service provider builds for all consumers) and treating the pattern as infrastructure work.
Hand-wrapping a generated client (gRPC stub, OpenAPI SDK) in a second full translation layer that only renames methods and adds nothing.
Hiding an N+1 loop behind one innocent-looking gateway method: iterating over a list and making one remote call per item, with no batching or DataLoader, so latency grows linearly with list size.
Skipping contract tests: stubbing the connection with hard-coded fixtures and never verifying the mapping against the live service, so the gateway silently diverges from the real API as it evolves.
Exposing foreign identifiers (UUIDs, database keys, vendor-specific enums) in the gateway return type, so a caller that stores the ID is silently coupled to the foreign system's namespace.

Treating the gateway as a caching layer rather than a translation boundary: adding caching logic inside the gateway instead of in a decorator or separate cache-adapter, mixing cache policy with vocabulary mapping.
design_principles: Separation of concerns: translating a foreign API is one responsibility, kept apart from application policy and business rules.
Dependency inversion: clients depend on the gateway's domestic interface, never on the vendor SDK, transport types or foreign error model.
Information hiding / least knowledge: the foreign vocabulary is not allowed to spread past the boundary it entered at.
Single responsibility: one gateway per cohesive external context, so its interface stays focused and its owner is unambiguous.
Open/closed principle: foreign changes are absorbed by extending the gateway internals instead of editing every call site.
Interface segregation: expose only the operations the application actually uses, not a mirror of the foreign API surface.
best_practices: Design the interface first, in domestic terms; translate arguments, results and errors at the edge rather than bending callers to the foreign shape.
Separate the connection object from the translation and inject it (constructor parameter, factory or DI container): it is simultaneously the configuration point and the test seam.
Keep the gateway to translation only; put retry/fallback policy in the connection or a decorator, and business rules in the caller.
Stub the connection in unit tests and keep at least one contract test against the real counterpart so the mapping stays honest.
Map foreign responses into your own types and ignore unknown fields (tolerate new ones), so external evolution cannot break the domain.
Expose coarse-grained operations where a caller would otherwise loop, and never hide an unbounded number of remote calls behind one method.
Make failures explicit in the domestic vocabulary: one error type or error enum that distinguishes transport, HTTP/status, protocol and payload failures.
Use a per-request context or DataLoader-style batcher when the gateway must make multiple downstream calls for one operation, to prevent N+1 query patterns.
Define the gateway's port interface in pure domestic terms; never expose vendor DTOs, raw JSON payloads or foreign identifiers in the public signature.
Version the gateway interface explicitly (e.g., BookingGatewayV2) and gate new behaviour behind a feature flag or constructor parameter rather than letting it grow without bound.
Apply circuit-breaker and rate-limit logic in the connection layer, not in the gateway translation logic, so the same retry/isolation policy works for all operations.
Prefer one gateway per cohesive bounded context or external system, not one gateway per method; co-locate translation for related foreign concepts to keep ownership clear.
When multiple clients call the same external service, share the gateway but not the connection: inject a per-request or per-tenant connection so tests can isolate callers.
Audit field-level mapping explicitly in code: name each translated field rather than using generic marshalling, so a reviewer can spot drift or omissions.
